[p. 59, paragraph after Figure 4:] Whilst the line is fuzzy, because not all of the isoglosses meeting to form one strong division, there is a clear difference between the southern isolects and Wanci and Kaledupa. The realisation of stressed syllables is interesting in the Wanci dialect. Rather than representing a prominence in the word manifested by pitch and loudness, stressed syllables seem to have acquired a consistently high, level pitch as their primary cue, rather than having a pitch change that is led by the intonation pattern of the sentence and co-occurs with increased loudness, as is the case in English and the other dialects.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states the position of word stress for Bonerate itself. Donohue 2000 treats Bonerate as an isolect of Tukang Besi and gives Bonerate-specific stress data only on the phonetic cue: the stressed syllable carries a falling pitch plus loudness ([\]), like Kaledupa/Tomea/Binongko and unlike Wanci's level high pitch; in the two-syllable example 'leg' ae the fall sits on the first (penultimate) syllable. The penultimate reading rests on that example plus the Tukang Besi rule in Donohue 1995 §2.3.2 p.29 (Wanci/Rupu speech): 'Stress is regularly assigned to the penultimate syllable of the word', and on the survey-level generalisations in Grimes & Grimes 1987 and Mead (Sulang 2016) that stress in these languages is predictable and penultimate. Treat as inferred, not stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Bonerate. For Tukang Besi (Donohue 1995 p.29): secondary stress on every second syllable preceding the primary-stressed penult.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Bonerate. Donohue 1995 p.30 (Tukang Besi) notes that a following article te is often counted as part of the verb for stress assignment, and gives mora-based rules for words with adjacent vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; Donohue 2000's data are elicited word-list forms (citation forms). The Figure 3/4 marks are pitch contours on the stressed syllable, not stress-position statements.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog/Ethnologue treat Bonerate (bone1254, bna) as a separate language, but Donohue (1995, 2000, 2004) and Mead (2003) treat it as a southern isolect/dialect of Tukang Besi (tuka1249 Tukang Besi South; Donohue 2000 gives 79-85% cognate with the four Tukang Besi islands). All stress statements found are for Tukang Besi proper (Wanci/Kaledupa speech, tuka1248/tuka1249), not for the Bonerate variety; Donohue 2000's Bonerate data are from Friberg's SIL word list and Donohue's own notes. Dialects per Grimes & Grimes 1987: Bonerate and Karompa (islands Bonerate, Karompa, Madu; not Kalaotoa).

sources.note: Treats Bonerate as an isolect of Tukang Besi (79-85% cognate). Fig. 3 (p.58) has a 'Stress' column: Wanci [ˉ] vs Kaledupa, Tomea, Binongko, Bonerate [\]; Fig. 4 (p.59) gives 'leg' ae [\_] for the southern isolects; text p.59 says stressed syllables in dialects other than Wanci show a pitch change plus increased loudness. Nothing on the POSITION of stress for Bonerate; the 215-item Bonerate word list (pp.64-72) writes apostrophe for glottal stop and marks no stress.
